episode_title: The WRONG Way to Fight Extremists

stories.topic: OPEC: The Cartoon Cartel That Couldn't
stories.summary: OPEC was the most brazen price-fixing club imaginable, and because its members were governments rather than firms, no antitrust law could touch it. After the Arab countries lost the 1973 war to Israel, a furious group of oil producers cut output by only 8%, and the price jumped from about $1.5 to $11 a barrel. Later histories show the producers themselves thought this was reckless: big oil consumers might simply land an army and seize the Gulf oil fields. Henry Kissinger is believed to have written a pseudonymous magazine article laying out exactly such an operation. No invasion came, and the cartel took shape. Ajay then runs the numbers. Oil went from $11 in 1974 to about $77 in 2023, roughly 7x, which is about 4% a year in nominal dollars and only about 1.5% a year in real terms. He gives three reasons. First, demand adjusts over the long run. Second, countries refuse to be extorted. Third, the cartel could not hold together: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar have small populations and could afford to cut supply, while populous Iran and Iraq kept pumping, and North Sea, Russian and Mexican oil filled any gap.
stories.insight: Even the most powerful cartel in history could not beat time. Short-term pain gives way to long-term adjustment, and members with different needs cheat on each other.
stories.quote: you tell me that you've got this powerful cartel that's controlling the price, and all they've managed to get is about one and a half percent real of a price hike

stories.topic: Reverse OPEC: India and China Become a Buyers' Cartel
stories.summary: When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Putin's implied threat was to leave Europe shivering through the winter by cutting off energy. Europe called the bluff and found a whole range of alternatives. Russian crude shifted to India (about 51% of its sales) and China. The West then invented a new tool of economic statecraft: a $60-a-barrel cap on Russian oil. It could be enforced because almost all of the world's shipping and shipping insurance is run out of Western countries, especially the UK, so shippers and insurers could be punished for handling Russian oil sold above $60. Ajay doubted it would work, since shadow tanker fleets would spring up (the FT reported one operating out of Bombay), but the data suggest it did. Putin needed money for the war and had only two big buyers left, so India and China gained the power to drive a hard bargain.
stories.insight: In fifty years the story came full circle: a sellers' cartel pushed prices up after the 1973 war, and a buyers' cartel pushed them down after the 2022 war. Leverage can also sit in unexpected places. Whoever controls the shipping and insurance can set the terms of a trade between two other countries.
stories.quote: So suddenly, instead of OPEC being a cartel of sellers, you had China and India as a cartel of buyers.

stories.topic: Ram Guha and the Best Bookshop on Church Street
stories.summary: In Bangalore, Amit stays on Church Street. It has the Takshashila Institution studio where he records, a Starbucks, and Blossoms, his favourite bookshop in the world, which makes it 'the best street in the world.' After recording a Seen and the Unseen episode with Ram Guha, Amit said he was off to the best bookshop in the world. Guha, in Amit's admittedly embellished retelling, called him a fool and said Blossoms wasn't even the best bookshop on Church Street, then took him to Bookworm. Amit visited both. Bookworm turned out to stock a copy of his own book, which settled the matter. It was later, in Blossoms' secondhand section, that he found a hardback of Fred Kaplan's The Insurgents on sale. That book started the rabbit hole behind this episode's chapter on guerrilla warfare.
stories.insight: It is a lovely piece of self-deprecation. It also shows how one chance find in a secondhand bookshop can open up a whole field, with one book leading to thirty more.
stories.quote: it turned out Bookworm actually had a copy of a shitty book I wrote a decade and a half ago. So I immediately concluded Blossoms is better.

stories.summary: Drawing on David Devadas's book, Amit describes 2007 as a year of new beginnings. A new generation of Kashmiris was sick of the fighting and wanted ordinary lives as programmers, engineers and artists, and the 2003 Vajpayee-Musharraf talks had laid some groundwork. But the security apparatus was entrenched, and men who had fought on the front lines in the 90s were now senior officers. The incentives were perverse. Rewards were tied to how many heads you could collect, which led to innocent people being killed. Ordinary Kashmiris needed government permission for everything, which bred rent-seeking ('mai-baap multiplied') and extortion. In one case a 19- or 20-year-old refused to hand over his Tata Indigo to a security man and was imprisoned. The window closed, Pakistan stepped in, and things got worse.
stories.insight: A counterinsurgency run as 100% military, instead of 80% political, creates more militants than it removes. Imagining yourself in a Kashmiri boy's shoes makes the cost of alienating your own citizens very concrete.
stories.quote: when you think of it from a Kashmiri boy's point of view, you know, you've seen your older brother taken away by the security forces and he disappears.

stories.topic: Decalogue I: The Father Who Calculated the Ice
stories.summary: The first film of Krzysztof Kieślowski's Dekalog is built on the commandment 'Thou shalt not have any other god than me.' A scientist father ('very much like you,' Amit tells Ajay) has a young son who is waiting for the lake to freeze so he can go skating. The father tracks temperatures, weather reports and every other piece of data, and finally concludes that today, within the margin of error, it is safe. The boy goes skating, the ice cracks, and he dies. In the last shot the father stands by the lake, and in the distance a homeless man has lit a fire to warm his hands.
stories.insight: Amit insists the film is not anti-science but a lesson in humility. The world is deeply complex, and an engineer's confidence that everything can be figured out and calculated can go badly wrong.
stories.quote: this film doesn't have an anti-science message to me. Instead, it has an important humility message to me.

stories.topic: The Bicycle Shot: Show Don't Tell on Screen
stories.summary: In Kieślowski's A Short Film About Love, a young man in an apartment complex has a crush on a woman across the way and keeps creepily watching her through her window. He decides to go to her door, possibly while delivering the milk or papers, and ask her out. He rings the bell. A conventional film would show the door opening, the question and her answer. Instead the film cuts to a top-angle shot of him in the courtyard below, riding round and round on his cycle in sheer joy. Amit uses this scene to teach his writing students about show-don't-tell.
stories.insight: The strongest storytelling often leaves out the obvious beat and lets a single image carry the emotion, trusting the audience to fill in the rest.
stories.quote: it just shows him ringing the bell, and the next shot is he's down in the courtyard, and it's a top angle shot, and he's down in the courtyard going round and round on a cycle in sheer joy. And it just tells you everything.

recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Ajay opens the cartel chapter with Smith's line that men of the same profession seldom meet without trying to rig the price. The book is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the standard mental model of cartels as an ever-present threat, the very model the OPEC story then tests against the data.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned right after Ajay's account of the Russian oil price cap and the 'reverse OPEC'.
recommendations.reason: Amit says the five-hour-plus conversation is full of insights like the ones Ajay shared about Russian oil, for anyone who wants the longer version.

recommendations.creator: Fred Kaplan
recommendations.context: Amit found a discounted hardback in Blossoms' secondhand section, and it sent him down a rabbit hole on guerrilla warfare.
recommendations.reason: It is a recent book that covers Petraeus and later developments in counterinsurgency thinking. It also has the clean summary of Galula's step-by-step method that Amit reads out on the show.

recommendations.creator: David Galula
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'the Bible' of counterinsurgency literature. Galula fought in China and Algeria, was once imprisoned by Mao's men, and wrote the book in the 60s.
recommendations.reason: Its central point is that fighting insurgents is completely different from conventional war, captured in the fly-versus-lion metaphor and the principle that you must keep the people on your side.

recommendations.creator: T. E. Lawrence
recommendations.context: Cited as the origin of the description of this kind of warfare as 'eating soup with a knife'.
recommendations.reason: It is part of the early literature on guerrilla war that existed long before the US went into Vietnam and still failed to learn from it.

recommendations.item: Learning to Eat Soup with a Knife
recommendations.creator: John Nagl
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a great book' whose title borrows T. E. Lawrence's image.
recommendations.reason: It sits in the counterinsurgency canon Amit worked through after Kaplan and Galula, which convinced him that this kind of war is mostly a political problem.

recommendations.item: The Generation of Rage in Kashmir
recommendations.creator: David Devadas
recommendations.context: Amit's main source for how the Indian security apparatus mishandled Kashmir.
recommendations.reason: Devadas argues that 2007 was a moment of hope, with a new generation that wanted jobs and normal lives. He documents in detail how perverse incentives such as body-count rewards, rent-seeking and extortion wasted that moment and alienated people.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Srinath Raghavan
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
recommendations.context: Mentioned while acknowledging that the Kashmir problem has a complicated historical side.
recommendations.reason: Amit says he discussed the history of the Kashmir problem 'in great detail' in that episode.

recommendations.item: India, Pakistan, Kashmir: We Won't Need To Fight A War If We Can Win The Peace
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's own column, linked in the show notes, applying the counterinsurgency lens to Kashmir.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his argument that India treated Kashmir as a purely military problem and lost its people, when the job of the state is to serve its citizens rather than rule over them.

recommendations.item: A Tale Of Two Bandits: Naxals And The Indian State
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's companion column on the Naxal problem.
recommendations.reason: It applies Mancur Olson's roving-versus-stationary-bandit frame to India's Naxal areas. In many of them both the state and the Naxalites behaved like roving bandits, and in some it was the Naxals who settled in and provided services.

recommendations.creator: Mancur Olson
recommendations.context: Amit names it as the source of the roving-bandit and stationary-bandit framework.
recommendations.reason: It offers a useful way to think about what a state is and why legitimacy matters in places like the Naxal belt.

recommendations.item: The Indian Armed Forces (Episode 175 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lt Gen Prakash Menon
recommendations.context: Amit discussed Kashmir briefly with Menon, who he believes was once in charge of the army there.
recommendations.reason: It gives the army's side of the argument: Menon was sensitive about Kashmir and asked what the army was supposed to do if Pakistan sent its people in. Amit says he gets that, while still holding his own view.

recommendations.item: The Liberal Nationalism of Nitin Pai (Episode 318 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nitin Pai
recommendations.context: Amit mentions having 'a strong argument' with Nitin Pai about these questions in a recent episode.
recommendations.reason: It is a long-form debate on the tension between defending borders as a nation state and serving the people you claim as your own.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay brings up the book while arguing that India's security failures reflect a wider problem.
recommendations.reason: Its key idea is that failures of state capability in India are cross-cutting, not domain-specific. The same missing debate, checks and balances, and feedback loops hurt health, finance and security alike.

recommendations.creator: Tirthankar Roy
recommendations.context: Ajay's book of the week, by an economic historian he calls a deep thinker about India.
recommendations.reason: It tells the story of India's evolution through the lens of firms and markets. Ajay urges even a businessperson who has never read a book to pick it up. What struck him most was how little has changed, and he came away with new respect for the people of a hundred and a hundred and fifty years ago.

recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
recommendations.context: A series of ten roughly hour-long films on the Ten Commandments, commissioned by Polish television around the end of the 80s. Amit once put it on his Twitter list of favourite web series, which surprised people.
recommendations.reason: For Amit it is 'the pinnacle of cinematic storytelling,' even above Kieślowski's more famous Three Colors trilogy and The Double Life of Veronique. The films aren't directly about the commandments but are beautiful human stories, and Amit says everyone should see it.

recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
recommendations.context: One of two Dekalog stories expanded into a roughly 90-minute film.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece. Its bicycle-in-the-courtyard scene is the example he uses to teach his writing students show-don't-tell.

recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
recommendations.context: The other Dekalog story expanded into a longer film.
recommendations.reason: Amit names it alongside A Short Film About Love, and calls both of them masterpieces.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's view is that cartels and monopolies can't last when anyone is free to enter the market, because someone will always come along and disrupt them. Lasting monopolies exist only where the state restricts competition or hands someone an advantage. OPEC is the usual counterexample, but it is made up of state actors, not market players.
core_ideas.quote: a seeming monopoly is impossible to sustain. And the only times that monopolies or cartels form is when the state actually interferes to give someone an advantage.

core_ideas.concept: Stuck in the Short Run, Adaptive in the Long Run
core_ideas.explanation: Demand barely responds to price in the short term: if petrol doubles tomorrow, you still have to drive to work. Over time, though, people adjust dramatically. Higher prices pay for more exploration, more fuel-efficient cars and substitutes for oil. A price shock that looks like proof of cartel power is often just the short run talking.
core_ideas.quote: in the short term, the responsivity of demand to the change in prices is very small. In the long run, however, human beings adjust dramatically.

core_ideas.explanation: Using a supply chokehold as hard power is short-sighted, whether it is OPEC with oil, China with rare earths against Japan in 2012, or Russia with energy against Europe. Ajay's thought experiment: suppose the Indian state made every call centre refuse to work for JP Morgan. JP Morgan would struggle for three weeks, and then the world would permanently route around a supplier that misbehaves. Victims respond by reducing their exposure.
core_ideas.quote: It's done without the slightest sense that in a conflict the other guy gets a vote and people don't like to be extorted.

core_ideas.explanation: The 1972 Club of Rome report and the 'peak oil' scare both projected current consumption forward and predicted doom. Both left out the price system: scarcity raises prices, which spurs exploration, substitution and innovation. Lithium is not rare at all, since it is made in abundance in stars right after hydrogen and helium, and serious business plans for towing resource-rich asteroids back to Earth were nearly viable. Ajay never worries about running out of natural resources. The constraint he does worry about is global warming, because filling the air with CO2 is a real threat.
core_ideas.quote: And what was missing in that entire thinking was the word price.

core_ideas.explanation: One of Mao's generals put it this way, and it is the core of David Galula's method. As summarised by Fred Kaplan: push the insurgents out, hold the area, win the people's trust and cut their ties to the insurgents, replace the insurgents' political organisation, then mop up. Petraeus boiled it down to one question to ask before any operation. Amit's verdict is that India's approach in Kashmir was close to 100% military and treated the people like an occupied population.
core_ideas.quote: Will this operation take more bad guys off the street than it creates by the way it's conducted?

core_ideas.explanation: Galula's metaphor for why conventional armies struggle against guerrillas. Each side is built for a different kind of fight, so conventional force against insurgents is like swatting at flies that keep coming back.
core_ideas.quote: if a fly and a lion are fighting, the fly cannot deliver a knockout blow, and the lion cannot fly.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay recasts Petraeus's question in the maths of epidemics that COVID taught everyone. If each infected person infects more than one other person, the epidemic explodes. In the same way, if killing one militant creates even slightly more than one new militant, the insurgency grows without limit. Every operation should be judged by that ratio, not by body count.
core_ideas.quote: if in the process of killing one militant you create 1.01 militants on average, then you've had it because this thing will explode.

core_ideas.explanation: Mancur Olson's model: a roving bandit robs a village and leaves for good. A stationary bandit settles in and taxes the village year after year, so he has reasons to build infrastructure and keep rival bandits out. A state is often a stationary bandit. In many Naxal areas the state was absent, so both it and the Naxalites behaved like roving bandits, and in some places the Naxals were the ones who settled in and provided services.
core_ideas.quote: A stationary bandit is a bandit who comes, he robs a village, but he wants to stay there and keep robbing it because people are resources, they'll create more.

core_ideas.concept: If Kashmir Is Integral, Kashmiris Are Your Citizens
core_ideas.explanation: Amit is not arguing against fighting Pakistan-backed terrorists or defending borders. His point is that claiming a territory means owning a duty to its people. A state's job is to serve its people, not rule over them, and alienating them hands the insurgency its next recruits.
core_ideas.quote: if you're saying Kashmir is an integral part of India, I strongly believe that that means that Kashmiri people are Indian people, you have to treat them like your own citizens.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Turn the Military on Your Own People
core_ideas.explanation: Armies are built to deliver overwhelming lethality against an enemy, and their training, manuals, equipment and tactics are designed for that job. Ajay is deeply uncomfortable when that machinery is used inside India against its own population.
core_ideas.quote: the military is an institution that is designed to marshal unlimited, unbelievable levels of violence in order to achieve an objective.

core_ideas.concept: Fear Ends Debate, and That Produces Bad Policy
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls this the securitization of the Indian state. Once 'national security' is invoked, all questions are supposed to stop, in the same way that warnings of a crisis are used to shut down debate on financial policy. He wants a debate led by civilians that engages with the complexity of these questions. In the French experience in Algeria and the American experience in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, criticism and soldier-intellectuals like Petraeus changed how the forces behaved. Per Ajay's book with Vijay Kelkar, this missing intellectual capacity is a weakness across the whole Indian state, not just in security.
core_ideas.quote: War is too important to be left to the generals, and security is too important to be left to security people.

core_ideas.explanation: The Western way of war produces diaries, logs and books in which people mourn their mistakes and study their wins, and that literature is how armies improve. Big institutions change slowly. Ajay compares them to a battleship (Indian health) or a super tanker (financial regulation), and Amit worries that any existing army is an anachronism in fast-moving times. Ajay ties this to the middle-income trap: crude mobilisation of resources can lift a poor country to lower-middle income, but going further needs a culture of evidence, post-mortems and criticism.
core_ideas.quote: What is striking about the Western way of war is the extent of introspection.

core_ideas.concept: Winning the War, Losing the Occupation
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that even if Russia had captured Kyiv and killed Zelensky, it could never have won the counterinsurgency that followed, because Ukrainians clearly saw themselves as a separate people. Ajay says this was his baseline from the start of the invasion. Any plan to invade should be tested by asking what happens after the conventional victory.
core_ideas.quote: they would win and they would be holding the world's worst counter insurgency. It would make Afghanistan seem like a walk in the park.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit spent five years as a professional poker player. He defines gambling as weighing up the probabilities and making a bet, and by that definition talking to someone in a bar, buying a 'haunted' house at a discount and launching this show are all gambles. Ajay agrees that taking risks is part of life, but calls lotteries (where you lose on average) and reckless derivatives positions decision mistakes. Amit replies that it is still the individual's right to make those mistakes, and that the state should stay out.
core_ideas.quote: everything we do in our lives is gambling because after all, what is gambling? You suss up the probabilities and you make a bet based on that.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The Eight Queens Problem opens the show. Amit solves it on the chessboard 'in one feverish attempt. So, like well done to me.' Ajay, who once wrote a program to solve it in Fortran, can't even see it as chess any more: 'for me it's an n-queens problem, and I have lost the ability to think of it as a chess problem.'
On whether the Saudi oil minister was imagining nuclear fusion replacing oil, Ajay notes that fusion 'is always the great technology of the next 20 years and has always been and will always be.'
Amit recalls Ajay's earlier joke that Putin deserves a Nobel Prize for solving climate change, since his war set off a rush of European investment in renewables.

Amit pitches a Bollywood film: Akshay Kumar flies a spaceship to an asteroid made of lithium and brings it back. Ajay objects that lithium is plentiful on Earth, so you'd need a heavy element. Tantalum gets suggested, and Ajay admits he just picked a name off the periodic table, which has 'all kinds of beautiful names' like yttrium.
Amit on his love for Blossoms' secondhand section: 'if you want to go for a week to Bali, I'll go for a week to Blossoms.'
In the gambling debate, Ajay says 'Lotteries are a tax on dumb people.' Amit replies: 'I would argue for the autonomy of dumb people... who's to decide who is dumb and who is not?'
Amit's sign-off: 'It's been a gamble on your part to watch it, and if you're still here, you've enjoyed it, right? So well done, you're a gambler.'

Adam Smith, as Ajay paraphrases him: 'men of the same profession seldom get together in the same room without trying to rig the price.' Ajay uses it to state the standard mental model of cartels before showing how OPEC fell short of it.

Saudi oil minister Ahmed Zaki Yamani: 'the Stone Age did not end because the world ran out of stones.' The oil age will end through technological change, which Ajay says is now happening through decarbonisation. He adds that Siberian gas may still be sitting in the ground a thousand years from now.

Henry Kissinger is believed to have written a pseudonymous magazine article in the 1970s detailing a military operation to seize the Persian Gulf oil fields and turn them into a global trust. It reflected a real fear among the OPEC producers themselves.
Bob Dylan, 'one of our heroes': Amit quotes 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall' as rain pours down outside the recording.
Ajay recalls Bloomberg building stock market indexes for each vice, picking listed companies that profit from things like gambling. This is what set off Amit's rant that all of life is gambling.
